transcript.content: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi. Nice to meet you too. Um, I'm here because... well, I just can't stop seeing this droop and unevenness around my mouth and my jaw. 

Every time I catch a reflection or see a photo of myself, it's all I can focus on. People keep telling me I look fine, but... it just feels so incredibly obvious to me. It's gotten so bad that I've actually started avoiding client meetings and presentations at work, so I knew I needed to come in and talk to someone.
How certain are you that the droop and unevenness are truly noticeable to other people?

Well, like I was saying, people do tell me I look fine. So I hear them when they say that. But... to me, I'm just absolutely certain it's there. It's glaring. 

Whenever I see a photo or catch my reflection, that droop is literally the only thing I can see. It feels so incredibly obvious that I just assume everyone else must be noticing it too, even if they're just being polite. That's exactly why I've been backing out of my client meetings and presentations at work. I just can't stand up in front of people feeling like they're staring at my uneven jaw.
Can you consider that your perception of the droop might be exaggerated or not actually noticeable, or are you completely convinced it is truly there?

I know what you're asking, but... no, I'm completely convinced it's there. I mean, I hear what people say, but I just can't stop seeing it. Every single time I look in a mirror or see a picture, the droop around my mouth and the unevenness in my jaw is right there. It's so obvious to me. It's why I can't face clients or do presentations anymore. I just can't shake the feeling that it's glaringly obvious, no matter what anyone else says.
How often do you check mirrors or photos specifically to inspect the droop or unevenness around your mouth and jaw?

It's a lot. Honestly, before I leave for work or if we have any kind of family event, I can spend hours just checking the bathroom mirror. I'll take pictures on my phone from different angles to see how it looks, and then I end up redoing my makeup or adjusting my scarf trying to hide it. 

I also ask my husband constantly if my face looks lopsided... and I'll even sit there scrolling through photos of other women just to see how bad my jaw looks beside theirs. So, it takes up a huge amount of my time.

When you avoid meetings and presentations, is it mainly because of your concern about the perceived droop and unevenness, or because you generally fear being judged or embarrassed in social situations?

It's definitely because of my face. I mean, I've been an architect for years, so I'm completely used to presenting designs and running client meetings. I never used to have a problem with it, and I don't have a general fear of talking to people or being judged on my work. 

It's really just... I can't stand the thought of them sitting there staring at my mouth and my uneven jaw while I speak. If my face didn't look like this, I'd be in those meetings right now without a second thought. So, yeah, it's strictly because of the droop.
Aside from your concern about your mouth and jaw, do you have any other beliefs that people around you say are clearly untrue?

No, not at all. It's just... it's just my face. I don't have any other strange beliefs or anything like that. People don't tell me I'm making things up about other stuff. It's really only when I talk about how my mouth and jaw look that my husband or my friends tell me I'm wrong. But other than that, no.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has an intense preoccupation with a perceived facial defect that others consider absent or minimal, accompanied by extensive mirror checking, photo-taking, reassurance seeking, camouflage behaviors, and marked occupational avoidance. The concern is appearance-specific rather than a generalized fear of social evaluation. Fixed conviction raises consideration of delusional disorder, somatic type, but the repetitive body-focused behaviors and appearance preoccupation most strongly support body dysmorphic disorder, with absent insight or delusional beliefs.
